extracted.intended_audience: researchers, geometers, and advanced students of analytic/projective geometry (19th-century mathematical readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Deriving and using analytic formulae and constructions in three-dimensional analytic geometry with oblique axes; and historical/projective-construction methods for polygons and conics (Brianchon, Poncelet, Gergonne, Servois, Rochat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of perspective projection as heuristic and provisional proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspective projection (projection of figures) may be used to demonstrate theorems respecting plane figures and furnishes unquestionable evidence of the truth of such theorems when correlatives for the circle have been proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projection is often treated as a kind of 'geometrical trickery' but provides strong evidence and guidance for searching systematic demonstrations; after using projection as an experimental/heuristic device, one should 'remount to first principles' to obtain a legitimate logical proof. Treat projection as evidence superior to physical experiment but ultimately seek rigorous demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use heuristic methods only as a guide to rigorous proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods that help 'get at' a general truth (e.g., projective or descriptive procedures) are legitimate but must be followed by a simpler or recognised mode of ultimate demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators who adopt general processes should seek simpler, recognised modes of ultimate demonstration and carefully scrutinize particular cases to avoid vagueness or erroneous assumptions introduced by reasoning about undelineated (not-drawn) figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check particular cases and data-dependence (including parity effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular variations in the hypotheses or data (for example, whether the number of polygon sides is odd or even) can render a generally true construction indeterminate or impossible in special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying general constructions, examine special cases (e.g., parity of number of sides) and follow the movement in a diagram to detect cases of impossibility/indeterminateness; these special cases deserve careful attention and must be handled explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit poles and polars / principle of duality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the doctrine of poles and polars (duality between points and lines) to convert inscribed/circumscribed polygon problems into dual problems which often admit cleaner constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply dual constructions (e.g., the dual of an inscribed polygon problem is a circumscribed polygon problem) and use polars to determine tangents, poles, and corresponding constructions. The method often reduces a complex problem to tangency/polar constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When required, perform constructions by straight lines only (ruler-only constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some posed problems specify that the operation 'shall be performed by means of straight lines only' (i.e., ruler-only constructions), excluding the use of compass or other instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the problem statement demands ruler-only construction, adopt constructions (such as Brianchon's or Rochat's linear procedures) that produce poles, tangents, and required intersections using straight lines and projective relations; ensure each step respects the ruler-only constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence condition for constructions: intersection/tangency requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A construction method yields a valid solution only when lines found by the prescribed method actually meet (or touch) the conic; if the constructed lines do not meet/touch the curve, the problem cannot be constructed and no polygons exist fulfilling all conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that lines produced by the method intersect the conic in the required points (tangency/contact conditions); coalescence of polygons corresponds to touching, and failure to meet indicates impossibility of the construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect degenerate / illusory data (e.g., concurrent given lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain degenerate data configurations (for example, when the three given lines meet in a single point) make the construction illusory or impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attempting the full construction, check for degenerate configurations of the given data (concurrency, coincidences) and treat such cases separately as they may invalidate the general construction or make steps (like determining poles) meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct equation to a plane via normal length and directing cosines
rubrics_metrics.description: The equation to a plane can be obtained by letting p be the length of the normal from the origin and l,m,n its directing cosines: the orthogonal projection argument leads to the plane equation Az + By + Cz = D with coefficients proportional to p and the directing cosines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive the plane equation by projecting any point of the plane onto the normal and equating projections; note that the absolute term and coefficients of variables are proportional to the length and directing cosines of the normal, a fact that holds for rectangular or oblique axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute normal length and directing cosines from plane coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the plane equation Az + By + Cz = D, the length p of the normal and its directing cosines l, m, n can be determined by algebraic relations obtained by equating coefficients (formulas (51), (52), (53) in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply appropriate auxiliary equations and equate coefficients to solve for p and the directing cosines; substitute back into the projection relation to determine K (and hence p) explicitly before finding l, m, n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find equations of the normal to a given plane (projecting coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: The equations to the normal (projecting coefficients) of a plane are given by explicit formulae (displayed as (55) in the text) expressing the projecting coefficients in terms of A, B, C and the metric parameters of the axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the derived expressions for the projecting coefficients (K l, K m, K n) in terms of the plane coefficients and the oblique-axis metric quantities; these determine the projecting coefficients of the normal and hence the normal direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of the plane perpendicular to a given line through a specified point
rubrics_metrics.description: Given equations of a straight line (directing/projecting coefficients), the plane perpendicular to it and passing through a given point (a, b, c) has equation obtained by using the line's directing cosines as the normal's cosines (formulas (57), (59)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form the plane equation by taking the directing cosines (or proportional quantities S,T,U) of the line and using them as coefficients (with appropriate metric combinations) in the linear equation through the given point; follow the algebraic substitutions shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute angles between a plane and coordinate planes via directing cosines
rubrics_metrics.description: The angles which a plane makes with the coordinate planes are equal to those which its normal makes with the normals to the coordinate planes; cosines (and sines) of these angles are computable via the plane's directing cosines and the metric factors (formulas (70) and (71)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the sign/magnitude conventions explained (choose the shorter revolution and positive sine for angles < 180°) to determine both magnitude and sign of the cosines and sines; use the explicit relations to avoid ambiguity inherent in supplementary angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance (perpendicular) from a point to a plane
rubrics_metrics.description: The perpendicular distance P from a point (a,b,c) to the plane Az + By + Cz = D is given by the orthogonal projection formula P = (A a + B b + C c - D) / sqrt( ... ) (explicit relation derived from projection argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the numerator as the value of the plane equation at the given point minus D, and divide by the appropriate normalization involving the oblique-axis metric factors (the same K or denominator used in earlier normal computations). For coordinate planes, the corresponding specialized values simplify the denominator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle between a straight line and a plane
rubrics_metrics.description: The required angle is the complement of that between the line and the normal; sin θ = (l'² + m'² + n'²)^(1/2) where l', m', n' are projecting coefficients (refer to formula (63) and subsequent substitutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the projecting coefficients of the line and use the plane's directing cosines to form the dot-product relations; substitute previously found K and metric quantities to get the explicit sine (or cosine) expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle between two planes (using normals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals; cos θ is given by a quadratic bilinear expression in the plane coefficients and metric factors (displayed as formula (68)), and sin² θ by the expression in (69).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute directions of normals via the projecting/directing-coefficient machinery, then apply the provided bilinear formulae to get cos θ and sin² θ; note that K (normalizing factor) for each plane appears in these formulae and must be computed consistently.
